q.why: 第二段：What made Steamboat Willie a sensation was sound。

q.q: When did the film's US copyright expire?
opts: November 18, 1928
January 1, 2024
It has not expired
q.why: 第四段：its copyright expired on January 1, 2024。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “debut” means ___.
opts: a final show before retiring
a first public appearance
a kind of theatre or cinema
a type of cartoon mouse
q.why: debut = 首次登場。

q.q: Why can't people use every version of Mickey freely?
opts: The 1928 film itself is still protected by copyright
Later versions are protected, and Mickey is a trademark
Ub Iwerks, the animator, still owns Mickey Mouse
The public domain only lasts for a single day
q.why: 最後一段：Later versions … are still protected, and Disney keeps Mickey as a trademark。

q.q: A shop sells T-shirts with the 1928 Mickey and the words “Official Disney Product.” Based on the text, what is the problem?
opts: Nothing is wrong, because the 1928 Mickey is in the public domain
T-shirts are not allowed to show any cartoon characters at all
The shop must use the later colour version of Mickey instead
The drawing is fine, but the 'official' claim misuses the trademark
q.why: 最後一段：people cannot pretend their products come from Disney。

tr.en: Walt Disney voiced Mickey himself, while his partner Ub Iwerks led the animation.
tr.zh: 華特・迪士尼親自為米奇配音，他的夥伴烏布・艾沃克斯則負責主導動畫。

tr.en: Nearly a century later, the film made headlines again.
tr.zh: 將近一個世紀後，這部影片再度登上新聞頭條。

tr.en: That does not mean anyone can use Mickey freely.
tr.zh: 這不代表任何人都能隨意使用米奇。

c.title: A Mouse, a Whistle and the Public Domain
text: On November 18, 1928, a seven-minute cartoon premiered in New York and quietly redrew the boundaries of popular entertainment. Steamboat Willie was not technically Mickey Mouse's first film, but it was the first to be released, and its tightly synchronised soundtrack turned a cheerful, whistling rodent into a phenomenon.

Its genius was technical as much as artistic. Walt Disney, who voiced the character himself, and his animator Ub Iwerks timed every gesture to music and sound effects, persuading audiences that the drawings were genuinely making noise.

From that modest premiere grew one of the most valuable brands in history, and with it a long political struggle over how long creative works should remain private property. American copyright terms were extended more than once in the twentieth century, extensions critics nicknamed the 'Mickey Mouse Protection Act'.
Yet time eventually won. On January 1, 2024, the original Steamboat Willie entered the US public domain, free for artists and teachers to reuse and reimagine.

The limits matter. Later versions remain protected, and trademark law still prevents anyone from implying a product is made by Disney. The episode illustrates the bargain at copyright's heart: creators deserve rewards, but culture also needs a common store of works that everyone can build upon.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Steamboat Willie was the first film ever made with Mickey Mouse in it.
Sound made Mickey a phenomenon; the public domain shows copyright's balance.
Copyright on famous works like Mickey should really last forever.
Sound made Mickey a phenomenon, and copyright on him should now last forever.
q.why: 主旨：音效讓米奇爆紅；進入公共領域體現著作權的平衡。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “implying” means ___.
opts: suggesting without saying directly
proving something with evidence
drawing a short cartoon
paying a fee to use something
q.why: implying = 暗示。

q.q: Why did critics call copyright extensions the 'Mickey Mouse Protection Act'?
opts: Mickey Mouse was named as the author of the law
The law was written by Walt Disney himself to protect real mice
The law was meant to end copyright altogether
They seemed to keep Disney's famous works private longer
q.why: 第三段：延長著作權年限被批評是在保護迪士尼的米奇。

q.q: How does the writer present copyright?
opts: As completely bad for everyone involved
As unimportant to the history of film
As a balance between creators and culture
As an invention of the Disney company
q.why: 最後一段：creators deserve rewards, but culture also needs a common store。

q.q: What is the purpose of the phrase “Yet time eventually won” in paragraph 4?
opts: To mark a turn: the film finally became public
To describe a race against the clock
To explain how synchronised sound works
To show that Disney's copyright on the film will never end
q.why: Yet 表轉折：儘管一再延長，作品終究進入公共領域。

q.q: A student makes a new short video using clips of the 1928 Steamboat Willie and posts it for a school project. Based on the essay, is this acceptable?
opts: No, because Mickey can never be used by anyone
Only if the student also uses the later colour versions
Yes, as long as it doesn't suggest Disney made it
Only if Disney gives written permission for the clips
q.why: 第四、五段：1928 版已屬公共領域，但不能暗示是迪士尼出品。

discuss: Why do you think a whistling mouse became so popular in 1928?
Should famous characters belong to their creators forever, or become free for everyone after some time? Why?
If you could reuse an old story or character for a new project, which one would you choose?

topic: World Toilet Day
zh: 世界廁所日：一間廁所的大學問

a.title: Why Toilets Matter
text: November 19 is World Toilet Day. It sounds funny, but it is a serious day.
Many of us use a clean toilet every day. But billions of people in the world do not have a safe toilet at home.
Without toilets, dirty water can get into rivers and drinking water. This can make people very sick, especially children.
Some girls stay home from school because their school has no clean, private toilet.
A man from Singapore named Jack Sim started this day in 2001. In 2013, it became an official UN day.
Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A funny day full of jokes about toilets
How Jack Sim became famous in Singapore
Why toilets are a funny subject for a holiday
Why safe toilets matter for health and school
q.why: 全文說明安全廁所對健康與上學的重要。

q.q: What can happen without toilets?
opts: Rivers and lakes slowly become cleaner
More children are able to go to school
Dirty water gets into drinking water
Families save money on their water bills
q.why: 第三段：dirty water can get into … drinking water. This can make people very sick。

q.q: When did World Toilet Day become an official UN day?
q.why: 第五段：In 2013, it became an official UN day。

q.q: In the text, “private” means ___.
opts: where other people cannot see you
very large, with lots of room for everyone
very clean and smelling fresh
full of clean, fresh water
q.why: private = 有隱私的。

q.q: Why do some girls stay home from school?
opts: They are tired of doing so much homework
They have to help clean the village river
Their school has no clean, private toilet
The school is too far away to walk to
q.why: 第四段：their school has no clean, private toilet。

q.q: Your school wants to help more girls in a poor village go to school. Based on the text, what is a good plan?
opts: Give each of the girls a new school bag only
Ask the girls to drink more water from the river
Start a fun day of toilet jokes at the school
Build clean, private toilets at the school
q.why: 第四段：沒有乾淨、有隱私的廁所會讓女孩不去上學。

gt.en: It sounds funny, but it is a serious day.
gt.zh: 聽起來很好笑，但這是一個嚴肅的日子。

gt.en: This can make people very sick, especially children.
gt.zh: 這會讓人生重病，特別是兒童。

gt.en: In 2013, it became an official UN day.
gt.zh: 2013 年，它成為聯合國正式的紀念日。

gt.en: Clean toilets protect our health, keep water clean, and help children go to school.
gt.zh: 乾淨的廁所保護我們的健康、維持水源乾淨，也幫助孩子上學。

b.title: The Invention That Saves Millions of Lives
text: World Toilet Day, held every November 19, began in 2001 when the Singaporean campaigner Jack Sim founded the World Toilet Organization. In 2013 the United Nations made it an official observance.

The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering. According to UN figures, around 3.5 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions have no toilet at all.

When human waste is not safely contained, it contaminates rivers, fields and drinking water. That spreads diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea, which remain major causes of death for young children in poorer countries.
Toilets also affect education and safety. Girls are more likely to miss school if there are no private, hygienic facilities, and women who must go outside at night can face danger.
Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step. Waste must also be collected and treated, or the problem simply moves downstream.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Safe sanitation, still missing for billions, is vital for health and school.
Jack Sim founded the World Toilet Organization in Singapore in 2001.
Toilets are an awkward subject that people would rather not discuss.
Safe sanitation now reaches almost everyone, so the day mainly celebrates success.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：數十億人缺乏安全衛生設施，而它攸關健康、教育與安全。

q.q: About how many people lack safely managed sanitation?
opts: 3.5 million
Everyone in poorer countries
Around 3.5 billion
q.why: 第二段：around 3.5 billion people。

q.q: Which diseases are mentioned as spreading from unsafe waste?
opts: Flu and colds
Cholera and diarrhoea
Diabetes and cancer
Polio and measles
q.why: 第三段：cholera and diarrhoea。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “sobering” means ___.
opts: funny, silly and light
funny, silly and easy to forget
serious and making you think
very small and minor
q.why: sobering = 令人警醒的。

q.q: What does “the problem simply moves downstream” mean?
opts: Toilets should always be built close to rivers
Rivers flow much faster once toilets are built
The problem simply disappears once toilets exist
Untreated waste still pollutes places further along
q.why: 最後一段：廢物沒處理，汙染只是移到下游。

q.q: A charity says: “We built 1,000 toilets, so the village's water is now safe.” Based on the text, what should you ask first?
opts: Is the waste collected and treated?
What colour are all the new toilets?
How many of the girls like the toilets?
When did Jack Sim start his organisation?
q.why: 最後一段：building toilets is only the first step. Waste must also be collected and treated。

tr.en: The topic makes some people giggle, but the numbers are sobering.
tr.zh: 這個主題讓一些人忍不住偷笑，但數字卻令人警醒。

tr.en: Toilets also affect education and safety.
tr.zh: 廁所也影響教育和安全。

tr.en: Experts stress that building toilets is only the first step.
tr.zh: 專家強調，蓋廁所只是第一步。

c.title: The Unglamorous Revolution
text: Few inventions are less celebrated or more consequential than the humble toilet. World Toilet Day, observed each November 19 and adopted by the United Nations in 2013, exists precisely because the subject is so easy to laugh off.

The scale of the shortfall is striking. Roughly 3.5 billion people lack safely managed sanitation, and hundreds of millions still have no facility at all. Where waste is not contained and treated, it seeps into water supplies and fuels diseases that kill hundreds of thousands of young children every year.

Historians of public health often argue that sanitation saved more lives than almost any medical breakthrough. The sewers built in nineteenth-century cities, prompted by deadly cholera outbreaks, transformed life expectancy long before modern drugs existed.
The consequences extend beyond disease. Without private, safe facilities, girls drop out of school and women face harassment; dignity itself is at stake.

Yet the solution is not merely to install more toilets. Without systems to collect and treat waste, sanitation simply relocates the problem. The real revolution is unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Sanitation is an overlooked problem that installing more toilets will completely solve.
Nineteenth-century sewers were the original cause of cholera in cities.
Sanitation is an overlooked foundation that needs whole systems, not just toilets.
Installing more toilets is the complete solution to the sanitation crisis.
q.why: 主旨：衛生設施影響重大卻被忽視，而且需要完整系統。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “consequential” means ___.
opts: very small and minor
having important results
easy to laugh at
very expensive to build
q.why: consequential = 影響重大的。

q.q: Why does the writer mention nineteenth-century sewers?
opts: Old sewers spread cholera, so modern cities should remove them
It explains exactly how cholera first began
It shows that toilets are a modern invention
Sanitation improved health even before modern drugs
q.why: 第三段：下水道在現代藥物出現前就大幅提升平均壽命。

q.q: Why does the writer call the revolution “unglamorous”?
opts: Its success depends on dull, unnoticed systems
Toilets are ugly and largely useless objects
Toilets are always dirty and unpleasant places
The United Nations does not support it at all
q.why: 最後一段：unglamorous infrastructure, quietly maintained。

q.q: How does the essay move from paragraph 2 to paragraph 3?
opts: From present-day numbers to history
From history to predictions about the future
From disease to the world of sport
From examples in Asia to examples in Africa
q.why: 第二段講現況數字，第三段用歷史證據支持。

q.q: A city has money for ONE project. Which choice best matches the essay's view?
opts: A famous new hospital full of the latest machines
Sewage collection and treatment for poor areas
A large statue celebrating the first flush toilet
Free toilet paper for every family for one year
q.why: 第三、五段：衛生系統（收集與處理）比單一醫療突破救更多人。

discuss: Why do you think people find it embarrassing to talk about toilets?
How do clean toilets at school affect students' learning?
What could your school or community do to keep water clean?

topic: Edwin Hubble and the Growing Universe
zh: 哈伯：發現宇宙正在變大的人

a.title: The Man Who Saw Other Galaxies
text: Edwin Hubble was born on November 20, 1889, in the United States. He became a famous astronomer.
An astronomer studies stars and space. Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California.
Long ago, people thought our galaxy, the Milky Way, was the whole universe. Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away.
He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!
Today, a space telescope has his name: the Hubble Space Telescope. It has taken amazing pictures since 1990.
Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The pictures taken by the Hubble Space Telescope
Edwin Hubble and what he found out about space
A tall mountain with a telescope in California
How a young person can become an astronomer
q.why: 全文介紹哈伯和他的發現。

q.q: What did people think long ago?
opts: That all galaxies were moving closer to us
That telescopes were not useful for science
That the Milky Way was the whole universe
That the universe was slowly getting bigger
q.why: 第三段：people thought our galaxy … was the whole universe。

q.q: When did the Hubble Space Telescope start taking pictures?
q.why: 第五段：It has taken amazing pictures since 1990。

q.q: In the text, an “astronomer” is a person who ___.
opts: builds tall mountains
takes photos of people
flies a spaceship to the Moon
studies stars and space
q.why: 第二段：An astronomer studies stars and space。

q.q: Why does the text say the universe is getting bigger?
opts: Most galaxies are moving away from us
The telescope on the mountain is very big
There are more new stars every single year
Hubble was born a long time ago, in 1889
q.why: 第四段：most galaxies are moving away from us. This means the universe is getting bigger!

q.q: Your friend says, “The Milky Way is everything in space.” Based on the text, what can you tell your friend?
opts: You are right — Hubble agreed with you
Hubble showed there are many other galaxies
The Milky Way is really a kind of telescope
Only scientists at NASA know the answer
q.why: 第三段：Hubble showed that there are many other galaxies far away。

gt.en: An astronomer studies stars and space.
gt.zh: 天文學家研究星星和太空。

gt.en: Hubble used a very big telescope on a mountain in California.
gt.zh: 哈伯在加州一座山上使用一架非常大的望遠鏡。

gt.en: He also found that most galaxies are moving away from us.
gt.zh: 他也發現大部分星系正在遠離我們。

gt.en: Hubble's work changed how we see our place in space.
gt.zh: 哈伯的研究改變了我們看待自己在宇宙中位置的方式。

b.title: Beyond the Milky Way
text: Edwin Hubble, born in Missouri on November 20, 1889, first studied law at Oxford before returning to his real passion: the stars.

In the early 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether fuzzy patches of light called nebulae were inside our galaxy or far beyond it. Using the giant Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson in California, Hubble measured special pulsing stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed that it was far too distant to belong to the Milky Way.
Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.

In 1929 Hubble published another landmark result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us. This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding. The Belgian scientist Georges Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier, which is why the rule is now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law.
In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hubble showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.
Hubble studied law at Oxford before he turned to astronomy instead.
Lemaître built the giant Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson in California.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit back in 1929.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：證明其他星系存在、宇宙在膨脹。

q.q: How did Hubble show Andromeda was outside the Milky Way?
opts: He took photos with the Hubble Space Telescope in 1990
He read Lemaître's paper and agreed with it
He measured pulsing stars and found it too far away
He took pictures of it with the space telescope
q.why: 第二段：measured special pulsing stars … far too distant。

q.q: What did Hubble publish in 1929?
opts: Andromeda is a cloud of gas inside our galaxy
The universe is slowly shrinking over time
The Milky Way is the only galaxy that exists
Farther galaxies seem to move away faster
q.why: 第四段：the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “expanding” means ___.
opts: getting colder
getting bigger
staying the same
turning around
q.why: expanding = 擴張、變大。

q.q: Why is the rule now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law?
opts: Lemaître built the telescope Hubble used
The two scientists were brothers
NASA renamed the law in 1990
Lemaître proposed a similar idea earlier
q.why: 第四段：Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier。

q.q: A website says: “Hubble alone came up with the idea that the universe is expanding.” Based on the text, is this fair?
opts: Not fully — Lemaître proposed it two years earlier
Yes — nobody else had ever studied the question
Yes — the space telescope is named after him
No — Hubble studied law, not the stars
q.why: 第四段：勒梅特早兩年提出類似想法。

tr.en: Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.
tr.zh: 仙女座是一個獨立的星系，宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。

tr.en: This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding.
tr.zh: 這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。

tr.en: In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.
tr.zh: 1990 年，NASA 發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的工作。

c.title: How Big Is Everything?
text: A century ago, the most basic question in astronomy, how big the universe is, had no agreed answer. Many astronomers believed the Milky Way contained everything; the faint spiral 'nebulae' scattered across the sky were assumed to be clouds within it.

Edwin Hubble, born on November 20, 1889, settled the dispute. In 1923, working with the great Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, he identified a Cepheid variable, a star whose regular pulsing reveals its true brightness, in the Andromeda nebula. Comparing true and apparent brightness yielded a distance far beyond our galaxy's edge.
The implication was staggering: Andromeda was an 'island universe', and the cosmos contained countless such galaxies.

Six years later he went further, showing that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. The universe was not static but expanding, a conclusion the Belgian priest-physicist Georges Lemaître had already reached theoretically, which is why astronomers now speak of the Hubble–Lemaître law.

Hubble never won a Nobel Prize, which did not then recognise astronomy. Yet his findings demoted humanity twice, from the centre of a single galaxy to one corner of an expanding cosmos, and few scientific discoveries have so thoroughly rescaled our sense of home.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Hubble's main achievement was finally winning the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Hubble proved the Milky Way is the whole universe, which made humans feel more central.
Hubble revealed countless galaxies in an expanding universe, shrinking our place.
The Milky Way, as people once thought, contains everything in the universe.
q.why: 主旨：無數星系＋宇宙膨脹，徹底改變人類的定位。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “recede” means ___.
opts: grow brighter
move away
stop moving
explode
q.why: recede = 後退、遠離。

q.q: Why was the Cepheid variable star so useful?
opts: It was simply the brightest star in the whole night sky
It was located safely inside our own Milky Way galaxy
It proved once and for all that the universe is static
Its regular pulsing shows its true brightness, so distance
q.why: 第二段：its regular pulsing reveals its true brightness——比較真實與視亮度可推算距離。

q.q: How does the writer view Hubble's lack of a Nobel Prize?
opts: A technicality that doesn't reduce his work
Proof that his work was really quite minor
Deeply unfair to the scientist Lemaître
A mistake made by NASA in naming the telescope
q.why: 第五段：諾貝爾獎當時不包含天文學，但他的發現依然極重要（Yet …）。

q.q: What does the phrase “demoted humanity twice” refer to?
opts: Two important prizes that Hubble failed to win
Two different telescopes that Hubble used
Two public arguments he had with Lemaître
Two discoveries that each made our place smaller
q.why: 結尾：從單一星系的中心，降為膨脹宇宙中的一角。

q.q: Which piece of evidence was MOST important for proving Andromeda is outside the Milky Way?
opts: A beautiful photo showing Andromeda's spiral shape
Distance worked out from a Cepheid's true brightness
Hubble's law degree from the University of Oxford
The size of the mirror in the Hooker telescope
q.why: 第二段：用造父變星的真實與視亮度算出距離，才證明它在銀河系之外。

discuss: How does it feel to know there are billions of galaxies? Does it make you feel small, or excited?
Hubble changed his career from law to astronomy. Is it good to change your path if you find a new passion?
Why do you think the space telescope was named after Hubble?

topic: World Fisheries Day
zh: 世界漁業日：海裡的魚還夠吃嗎？

a.title: Fish for Tomorrow
text: November 21 is World Fisheries Day. It reminds us to take care of the fish in our seas, rivers and lakes.
Fish are an important food for billions of people. Millions of people also work as fishers.
But some people catch too many fish. Then there are not enough young fish to grow up and lay eggs. This is called overfishing.
Today, more than one third of the world's fish groups are overfished.
Some fish now come from fish farms. Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.
If we only catch what the sea can replace, there will be fish for our children in the future.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why people should stop eating any fish from the sea
Why fish farms are always bad for the sea
Caring for fish so there are enough in future
A big fishing competition held every year
q.why: 全文談保護魚類，讓未來還有魚可吃。

q.q: What is overfishing?
opts: Eating fish for dinner every single day
Catching so many fish that too few grow up
Building lots of fish farms along the coast
Fishing only in rivers and not in the sea
q.why: 第三段：catch too many fish … This is called overfishing。

q.q: How much of the world's fish groups are overfished?
opts: More than one third
Less than one tenth
All of them
Exactly a half
q.why: 第四段：more than one third。

q.q: In the text, “replace” means ___.
opts: throw something away in the bin
sell something at the market
catch something faster than before
put back or grow again what was taken
q.why: replace = 補回。

q.q: What does the writer think about fish farms?
opts: They can help, but must be clean and careful
They solve every problem the oceans have
They are perfect and solve every problem at sea
They are really the same as overfishing
q.why: 第五段：Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too。

q.q: Your family is buying fish at the market. Based on the text, which choice helps the sea most?
opts: As many baby fish as you can find at the market
As much fish as possible while the price is low
Only fish that has come from very far away
Fish caught in a way that lets young fish grow
q.why: 第三、六段：讓小魚長大，只捕大海能補回的量。

gt.en: Fish are an important food for billions of people.
gt.zh: 魚是數十億人重要的食物。

gt.en: This is called overfishing.
gt.zh: 這叫做過度捕撈。

gt.en: Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.
gt.zh: 養殖場可以幫忙，但也必須乾淨又小心。

gt.en: If we only catch what the sea can replace, there will be fish for our children in the future.
gt.zh: 如果我們只捕撈大海能補回的量，未來我們的孩子就還有魚。

b.title: Can the Oceans Keep Feeding Us?
text: World Fisheries Day, celebrated on November 21, was started in 1997 by fishing communities who met in New Delhi to call for responsible fishing around the world.
Fish and seafood are a major source of protein for billions of people, and fishing supports the jobs of tens of millions more, from small boats to large factory ships.

However, the oceans are under pressure. According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of the world's fish stocks are now overfished, meaning they are caught faster than they can reproduce.
Illegal fishing, harmful methods that destroy the seabed, and bycatch, the accidental capture of dolphins, turtles and sharks, make the problem worse.
Fish farming, or aquaculture, now produces more than half of the seafood we eat. It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Fish feed billions, and new fish farms have now completely ended overfishing.
Fish feed billions, but overfishing threatens the seas, so care is needed.
Fish farming has now completely solved the problem of overfishing.
Dolphins and sea turtles are caught as food for millions of people.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：魚很重要、海洋受威脅、需要負責任的漁業。

q.q: What does “overfished” mean in the text?
opts: Fish are caught faster than they can breed
There are too many fish farms in one area
The fish being caught are much too big
Fish are caught only by small local boats
q.why: 第三段：caught faster than they can reproduce。

q.q: How much of our seafood now comes from aquaculture?
opts: About a tenth
None
More than half
Exactly a third
q.why: 第五段：now produces more than half of the seafood we eat。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “bycatch” means ___.
opts: fish that are sold at local markets
fish that are raised on fish farms
fish that are caught on purpose to sell at markets
animals caught by accident while fishing
q.why: bycatch = 混獲，意外捕到的動物。

q.q: Why does the writer say fish farms are not a perfect solution?
opts: They produce far too little fish to feed people
They often catch dolphins and turtles by accident
Poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters
They are against the law in most countries
q.why: 第五段：poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters。

q.q: A seafood ad says: “Eat all the farmed fish you want — it never harms the ocean.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: No — poorly run farms can pollute coastal waters
Yes — fish farms never cause any harm to the ocean
Yes — fish farms produce half of our seafood
No — farmed fish are not really fish at all
q.why: 第五段：管理不善的養殖場會汙染沿岸海水。

tr.en: However, the oceans are under pressure.
tr.zh: 然而，海洋正承受壓力。

tr.en: It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
tr.zh: 它能減輕野生魚類的壓力，但管理不善的養殖場會汙染沿岸海水。

tr.en: Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.
tr.zh: 專家說，解決方法包括捕撈限額、海洋保護區，以及更完善地追蹤魚的來源。

c.title: The Tragedy of the Open Sea
text: The ocean once seemed inexhaustible. Today, World Fisheries Day, marked each November 21 since 1997, serves as an annual reminder that it is not.

According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of assessed fish stocks are overfished, harvested faster than they can replenish themselves. The causes are partly technological: sonar, vast nets and subsidised fleets allow fishers to locate and remove fish with an efficiency earlier generations could not imagine.

Economists describe the dynamic as a 'tragedy of the commons'. Because no single fisher owns the sea, each has an incentive to catch as much as possible before others do, even though restraint would leave everyone better off.

Aquaculture has eased some pressure and now supplies most of the seafood humans eat, but it brings its own costs, including coastal pollution and, for some species, a reliance on wild fish ground into feed.

The most promising answers are institutional rather than technical: enforceable quotas, marine reserves where stocks can recover, and traceability that lets consumers reward responsible fleets. The sea can recover remarkably quickly, but only if people agree to share it.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Better fishing technology will, on its own, solve the overfishing problem.
Fish farming offers a way to feed people with no costs at all.
Overfishing is a shared-resource problem needing rules and cooperation.
The ocean is so vast that its fish can never really run out.
q.why: 主旨：這是公共資源問題，要靠可執行的制度與合作。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “incentive” means ___.
opts: a type of large fishing net
a law that limits fishing
a law that punishes people for fishing
a reason that encourages an action
q.why: incentive = 誘因。

q.q: Why does each fisher catch as much as possible, according to the 'tragedy of the commons'?
opts: Fishing has become very easy with modern boats
No one owns the sea, so each fears others will take it
Fish are cheap, so fishers must catch a lot
Quotas require each fisher to catch as much as possible
q.why: 第三段：no single fisher owns the sea … catch as much as possible before others do。

q.q: How does the writer view aquaculture?
opts: As helpful, but with its own costs
As a perfect solution for the seas
As completely harmful to the ocean
As illegal in most countries
q.why: 第四段：has eased some pressure … but it brings its own costs。

q.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
opts: Recovery is possible, but needs cooperation
The sea can no longer recover from fishing
Technology alone will save the world's fish
Consumers should simply stop eating fish
q.why: 結尾：can recover … but only if people agree to share it。

q.q: Three countries share one sea. Which plan best follows the writer's advice?
opts: Each country builds faster boats to catch more first
All three countries stop eating fish completely
Agree limits, set up a reserve, and track sales
They let each fisher decide how much to catch
q.why: 最後一段：enforceable quotas, marine reserves … traceability。

discuss: What kinds of fish or seafood does your family eat? Do you know where they come from?
Why is it hard to stop overfishing when the sea belongs to no one?
Taiwan has a big fishing industry. How could Taiwan protect both fishers' jobs and the ocean?

topic: King Midas and the Golden Touch
zh: 點石成金的邁達斯王

a.title: Be Careful What You Wish For
text: Long ago, in a Greek story, there was a king named Midas. He loved gold more than anything.
One day, Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
Midas said, 'I wish that everything I touch turns into gold!' His wish came true.
At first he was very happy. He touched a stone, a flower and a chair, and they all became gold.
But then he tried to eat. His bread and water turned into gold too! Midas was hungry and afraid.
He asked the god to take the gift back. Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How the king's cooks made bread and wine
A king whose golden wish caused trouble
A friend of the god Dionysus who got lost
Why gold is such a beautiful metal
q.why: 全文講邁達斯的點金願望帶來麻煩。

q.q: Why did the god give Midas a wish?
opts: Midas loved gold more than anything
Midas was very hungry and thirsty
Midas helped the god's friend
Midas was a god himself
q.why: 第二段：Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him …

q.q: What happened when Midas tried to eat?
opts: His bread and water turned into gold
His food began to taste much better
He became a god who could fly
He found even more gold in the river
q.why: 第五段：His bread and water turned into gold too!

q.q: In the text, “touch” means ___.
opts: look at something closely
eat something quickly
buy something at a shop
put your hand on something
q.why: touch = 碰觸。

q.q: What lesson did Midas learn?
opts: Gold is the most important thing of all
The gods never help ordinary people
Some things are worth more than gold
Wishes always make people happy
q.why: 最後一段：some things are worth more than gold。

q.q: A classmate says, “If I were rich, I would never have any problems.” What would Midas's story suggest?
opts: Money can't buy everything, like food and love
You are right — gold solves every problem
You should ask a god to give you money
You are right — being rich solves every problem
q.why: 故事寓意：金錢買不到所有真正重要的東西。

gt.en: He loved gold more than anything.
gt.zh: 他愛黃金勝過一切。

gt.en: To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
gt.zh: 為了感謝他，神給了邁達斯一個願望。

gt.en: His wish came true.
gt.zh: 他的願望實現了。

gt.en: Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.
gt.zh: 邁達斯學到，有些東西比黃金更有價值。

b.title: The Curse of the Golden Touch
text: In Greek mythology, Midas was a wealthy king of Phrygia who believed that more gold would bring him more happiness.

When Midas kindly looked after Silenus, the old teacher of the wine god Dionysus, the grateful god offered him any reward he desired. Without hesitating, Midas asked that everything he touched would turn to gold.

At first the gift seemed wonderful. Twigs, stones and apples glittered in his hands. But when he sat down to dinner, his bread hardened into metal and his wine became liquid gold. The richest man in the world was starving.
Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish. The god told him to wash in the River Pactolus, and according to the myth, that is why the river's sand sparkled with gold ever after.
In a famous later retelling by the American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, Midas even turns his beloved daughter into a golden statue — a detail that makes the warning hit harder.
Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The American writer Hawthorne wrote the very first story about Midas.
The River Pactolus is still full of gold that people can find today.
Midas's golden wish showed how greed destroys what truly matters.
Dionysus was the Greek god in charge of gold and wealth.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：貪婪的願望毀掉真正重要的東西。

q.q: Why did Dionysus offer Midas a reward?
opts: Midas gave the god a large gift of gold
Midas won a race against the other kings
Midas was really the god's own son
Midas looked after Silenus, his old teacher
q.why: 第二段：Midas kindly looked after Silenus。

q.q: How did Midas get rid of the golden touch?
opts: He gave all of his gold away
He washed in the River Pactolus
He broke the golden statue
He stopped eating and drinking
q.why: 第四段：wash in the River Pactolus。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “greed” means ___.
opts: wanting much more than you need
great kindness to others
deep and lasting sadness
wanting to share what you have with others
q.why: greed = 貪婪。

q.q: Why does the writer say Hawthorne's daughter detail “makes the warning hit harder”?
opts: Golden statues are very expensive to make
Losing someone he loved shows greed's true cost
Hawthorne was an American, not a Greek
Golden statues show how beautiful the king's wish was
q.why: 第五段：把心愛的女兒變成金像，貪婪的代價更沉重。

q.q: A news article praises a businessman for having “the Midas touch.” Based on the text, what is surprising about this phrase?
opts: Today it's praise, but the story warns against greed
It means the businessman is very kind to others
Today it's a warning, but the story praises greed
It means the businessman is a kind of god
q.why: 最後一段：今天是讚美賺錢能力，原故事其實是對貪婪的警告。

tr.en: At first the gift seemed wonderful.
tr.zh: 一開始，這份禮物看起來好極了。

tr.en: The richest man in the world was starving.
tr.zh: 世界上最有錢的人卻在挨餓。

tr.en: Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish.
tr.zh: 走投無路的邁達斯懇求戴奧尼索斯收回這個願望。

c.title: The Poverty of Gold
text: Few myths compress a moral so neatly as that of King Midas. Granted a wish by Dionysus in gratitude for sheltering the god's elderly companion Silenus, the Phrygian king asks that whatever he touches be turned to gold, and discovers at dinner that he has made himself unable to eat.

The story's force lies in its precise inversion. Gold is valuable precisely because it can be exchanged for other things; Midas, by converting everything into gold, abolishes the very things gold was meant to buy. His wealth becomes a form of poverty.

Ancient versions, preserved most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, end with Midas washing away his curse in the River Pactolus, an aetiological flourish explaining the gold-bearing sands of a real river.
Later tellers sharpened the tale. Nathaniel Hawthorne's nineteenth-century version adds a daughter who turns to metal at her father's embrace, shifting the moral from hunger to love.

Curiously, modern English has reversed the myth's meaning. To have 'the Midas touch' is now a compliment for commercial success, as though the cautionary half of the story had been quietly edited out — perhaps the most telling evidence of how persuasive the dream of endless wealth remains.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Midas was, above all, a successful king who knew how to make money.
Ovid invented the River Pactolus to explain where Midas's gold went.
The myth praises wealth, and our language has kept that meaning of praise.
The myth shows wealth becoming poverty, yet our language made it praise.
q.why: 主旨：財富變貧窮的寓言，現代英文卻把警告變成讚美。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “cautionary” means ___.
opts: very funny
about money
giving a warning
from ancient Rome
q.why: cautionary = 警示性的。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “His wealth becomes a form of poverty”?
opts: Turning all to gold destroys what gold should buy
Midas soon loses all of the gold that he has
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor people of his land
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor
q.why: 第二段：把一切變成黃金，反而消滅了黃金能買的東西。

q.q: How does the writer view the modern phrase 'the Midas touch'?
opts: As a correct summary of the myth's lesson
As an ironic reversal showing wealth's pull
As an insult to successful business people
As a phrase first used by Ovid himself
q.why: 最後一段：反轉神話原意——顯示無盡財富的夢多麼誘人。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4 (Hawthorne's version)?
opts: To prove that Ovid's version was wrong
To explain where the River Pactolus is
To show how retellings moved the moral to love
To show that Hawthorne kept Ovid's moral exactly the same
q.why: 第四段：shifting the moral from hunger to love。

q.q: An app promises: “Turn all your free time into money!” Based on the essay, what would be the strongest criticism?
opts: Turning everything into money can destroy rest and relationships
The app might not actually make you enough money in the end
Apps on phones are not really able to make money for anyone
The app might not actually turn enough of your free time into money
q.why: 第二段的邏輯：把一切換成金錢，反而失去金錢本來要換取的東西。

discuss: If you could have one magic power for a day, what would you choose — and could it go wrong?
What are some things that are 'worth more than gold' to you?
Why do you think people today use 'the Midas touch' as praise?

topic: World Children's Day: Rights for Every Child
zh: 世界兒童日：每個孩子的權利

a.title: Every Child Has Rights
text: November 20 is World Children's Day. On this day in 1989, the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children.
It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child. A right is something every person should have.
Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
Children also have the right to give their opinions. Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
Almost every country in the world has signed this promise. Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
But many children still cannot go to school or are not safe. World Children's Day reminds us to keep this promise.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How children should play games at school
World Children's Day and every child's rights
World Children's Day and the rights only adults have
How to see a doctor when you are ill
q.why: 全文介紹世界兒童日與兒童權利。

q.q: What happened on November 20, 1989?
opts: Taiwan made a new law about children
Every child in the world went to school
World Children's Day came to an end
The UN agreed on a promise for children
q.why: 第一段：the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children。

q.q: Which is NOT listed as a right in the text?
opts: To have their own car
To go to school
To play
To give their opinions
q.why: 第三、四段列出上學、安全、看醫生、玩、表達意見，沒有車子。

q.q: In the text, a “right” is ___.
opts: the opposite of the word left
a kind of game that children play
something every person should have
a rule that every school must follow
q.why: 第二段：A right is something every person should have。

q.q: Why does the day still matter today?
opts: Every child in the world can now go to school and is always safe
Many children still can't go to school or are not safe
The promise made in 1989 has now come to an end
Only adults, and not children, have any rights
q.why: 最後一段：many children still cannot go to school or are not safe。

q.q: Your school is choosing a new lunch menu. Based on the text, what should the school do?
opts: Decide quickly without asking any of the students
Let only the parents choose what children eat
Ask students, because the decision is about them
Choose the cheapest food without asking anyone
q.why: 第四段：Adults should listen when decisions are about them。

gt.en: A right is something every person should have.
gt.zh: 權利是每個人都應該擁有的東西。

gt.en: Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
gt.zh: 兒童有權上學、有權安全、有權看醫生，也有權玩耍。

gt.en: Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
gt.zh: 當決定和兒童有關時，大人應該聆聽。

gt.en: Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
gt.zh: 台灣也在 2014 年把它納入自己的法律。

b.title: A Promise to the World's Children
text: On November 20, 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and the date is now celebrated as World Children's Day.

The convention sets out the rights that every person under 18 should enjoy, wherever they live. They include the right to education, to health care, to protection from violence and exploitation, and, in a famous article, the right to rest and play.

One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected. They have the right to express their views on matters that affect them, and adults must take those views seriously.

It has become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history: every UN member state except the United States has ratified it. Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide. Millions of children are still out of school, working in dangerous jobs, or living through war.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The United States is the only UN member that has not ratified the convention.
The 1989 convention promises every child rights, but many still lack them.
Taiwan passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its legal system.
Children need protection from harm more than they need a voice in decisions.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：公約承諾權利與發聲，但現實仍有落差。

q.q: Who is a “child” under the convention?
opts: Anyone under 12
Only students
Every person under 18
Anyone who lives with parents

c.title: Rights Before Adulthood
text: For most of history, children were regarded less as people than as possessions, or as adults in waiting. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989, marked a decisive break with that view.

Its premise is that childhood carries rights of its own. Alongside protection from violence, exploitation and neglect, the convention guarantees education, health care and even rest and play, acknowledging that a good childhood is not merely survival.

Its most radical provision concerns participation: children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, with due weight given according to their age and maturity. This reframes children from passive recipients of care into people whose opinions count.

The treaty has been ratified by every UN member except the United States, making it the most widely accepted human rights agreement ever. Taiwan, excluded from the UN, incorporated it into domestic law in 2014, an example of how norms can spread beyond formal membership.
Ratification, however, is not realisation. Child labour, conflict and unequal schooling persist, a reminder that rights written on paper become real only when adults choose to honour them.

b.title: Rabbits, Sunflowers and a Famous Sequence
text: Every November 23, maths fans celebrate Fibonacci Day, because the date written as 11/23 matches the first four numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.

The sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and each number is the sum of the two before it. It takes its name from Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who described it in his book Liber Abaci in 1202 through a puzzle about breeding rabbits.

Fibonacci did not invent the sequence: Indian mathematicians had studied the same pattern centuries earlier. His bigger contribution was introducing the Hindu–Arabic numerals 0 to 9 to Europe, which made calculation far easier than Roman numerals.

The numbers appear surprisingly often in plants. Sunflower heads and pinecones usually have spirals that come in neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, an arrangement that packs seeds efficiently.

However, popular claims that the sequence is hidden in every famous building or 'perfect' face are usually exaggerated. Scientists warn that if you look hard enough, you can find patterns almost anywhere.

c.title: Patterns, Real and Imagined
text: Fibonacci Day, celebrated on November 23 because 11/23 echoes the opening of the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, honours one of mathematics' most beloved patterns, and offers a useful lesson in scepticism.

The rule is simple: each term is the sum of the two preceding ones. Leonardo of Pisa popularised it in Liber Abaci in 1202 through a whimsical problem about multiplying rabbits, though Indian scholars had described the same sequence far earlier. Ironically, his more consequential achievement was persuading European merchants to abandon cumbersome Roman numerals for the Hindu–Arabic system.

In botany the sequence earns its reputation. The spirals of sunflower heads and pinecones typically occur in adjacent Fibonacci numbers, because placing each new seed at a constant angle produces efficient packing; the mathematics emerges from growth rather than design.

Elsewhere, enthusiasm outruns evidence. Claims that the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa or ideal human faces encode the related golden ratio rarely survive careful measurement, and often depend on choosing convenient starting points.
The sequence therefore teaches two lessons at once: nature genuinely contains elegant regularities, and human minds are so eager for pattern that we readily invent ones that are not there.

b.title: The Book That Changed Biology
text: On November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. The first printing sold out almost immediately, and the book went on to transform how people understand life on Earth.

Darwin's ideas had been forming for more than twenty years. As a young naturalist on the survey ship HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, he collected fossils and observed animals in South America and on the Galápagos Islands, where species differed slightly from island to island.

His central idea was natural selection. Individuals vary, and those with traits that suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so over many generations species gradually change.

Darwin delayed publishing, partly because he knew his ideas would be controversial. He finally acted in 1858 when another naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, sent him a paper describing almost the same theory. Their work was presented together in London that year.
Today evolution is the foundation of modern biology, supported by evidence from fossils and DNA.

c.title: The Long Patience of a Revolutionary
text: On November 24, 1859, a cautious naturalist published one of the most consequential books ever written. On the Origin of Species argued that the diversity of life arose not through separate acts of creation but through descent with modification, driven by natural selection.

The argument had been decades in the making. Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle in the 1830s furnished him with puzzles, notably the subtly different finches and tortoises of the Galápagos Islands, but he spent the next twenty years accumulating evidence, breeding pigeons and corresponding with experts before daring to publish.

That reluctance was strategic as well as temperamental. He anticipated fierce religious and scientific opposition, and he wanted his case to be overwhelming. Only a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, outlining the same mechanism, forced his hand.

The book's power lay in its accumulation of ordinary observations into an extraordinary conclusion. Variation exists; more offspring are born than can survive; those best suited to their surroundings leave more descendants. Given immense time, small differences add up to new species.
Later discoveries in genetics, unknown to Darwin, supplied the mechanism of inheritance he lacked and confirmed the theory's core with striking precision.

b.title: Making a Fortune, Giving It Away
text: Andrew Carnegie, born on November 25, 1835, in Dunfermline, Scotland, is one of history's most famous examples of rags to riches.

His family emigrated to Pittsburgh in 1848, where twelve-year-old Andrew worked in a cotton mill for little more than a dollar a week. He moved on to a job as a telegraph messenger, impressed his bosses, and invested his savings wisely.
By the 1870s he had built a steel empire. In 1901 he sold Carnegie Steel for about 480 million dollars, making him one of the richest men alive.

Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away. In his essay The Gospel of Wealth, he argued that the rich have a duty to use their money for the public good during their lifetimes. He funded more than 2,500 public libraries around the world, as well as universities and concert halls.
His record is mixed, however. In 1892 a bitter strike at his Homestead steelworks ended in deadly violence, and critics argue that his generosity was paid for by workers' low wages and long hours.

c.title: The Contradictions of a Philanthropist
text: Andrew Carnegie, born in Scotland on November 25, 1835, embodied the American myth of the self-made man with almost theatrical neatness: a penniless immigrant boy who became the richest industrialist of his age.

His ascent combined diligence, shrewd investment and fortunate timing. From a cotton mill and a telegraph office he rose into railways and then steel, ruthlessly cutting costs until Carnegie Steel dominated the industry. Its sale in 1901 for roughly 480 million dollars made him almost unimaginably wealthy.

What followed was equally remarkable. In The Gospel of Wealth he contended that dying rich was a disgrace and that fortunes should be distributed for the public good. He funded more than 2,500 libraries, believing that access to knowledge, not charity handouts, allowed people to improve themselves.

Yet the same cost-cutting that built the fortune also produced the Homestead strike of 1892, in which a clash between strikers and armed guards left several people dead. Critics then and since have asked whether generosity can redeem wealth extracted from exhausted workers.
Carnegie's legacy thus resists a simple verdict, and it raises a question that remains urgent: should society rely on the goodwill of the very rich, or on fairer wages in the first place?

b.title: Good Grief: The Genius of Peanuts
text: Charles M. Schulz, born in Minneapolis on November 26, 1922, created one of the most popular comic strips in history. Peanuts first appeared in newspapers on October 2, 1950, and ran for almost fifty years.
Unusually, Schulz wrote, drew and lettered every one of the nearly 18,000 strips himself, without assistants.

His characters were children, but their worries were very adult. Charlie Brown is lonely and unlucky; Lucy is bossy; Linus carries a security blanket while thinking deep thoughts. Readers recognised their own fears and disappointments in these small figures.
Snoopy, Charlie Brown's beagle, provided the fantasy. Lying on top of his doghouse, he imagines himself as a fighter pilot or a famous novelist.
The strip grew into books, toys and television specials such as A Charlie Brown Christmas in 1965.
Schulz died in February 2000, just hours before his final Sunday strip was published. Today, his gentle mix of sadness and humour continues to influence cartoonists around the world.

c.title: The Comedy of Failure
text: Few artists have built a global empire on disappointment. Charles Schulz, born on November 26, 1922, spent nearly half a century chronicling the defeats of Charlie Brown, a boy who never wins a baseball game, never talks to the little red-haired girl and is always, inevitably, tricked by Lucy into missing the football.

That persistent failure was the strip's genius. Peanuts, launched in 1950, gave children the anxieties of adults, insecurity, loneliness and existential doubt, and allowed readers to laugh at feelings they rarely admitted to themselves.

Schulz's craftsmanship was stubbornly personal. He drew, wrote and lettered almost 18,000 strips without assistants, and the deliberate simplicity of his line concealed careful timing within the four panels.

Against Charlie Brown's realism stood Snoopy's boundless fantasy. The beagle who imagined himself a First World War flying ace or a struggling novelist offered an escape that complemented, rather than cancelled, the melancholy.

Schulz died in February 2000, hours before his final Sunday strip appeared, a coincidence his admirers found almost unbearably fitting. His enduring lesson is that resilience need not look heroic; sometimes it simply means trying to kick the football one more time.

b.title: From Traffic Jams to Global Sales
text: Black Friday falls on the day after Thanksgiving in the United States, which this year is November 27. For decades it has marked the unofficial start of the Christmas shopping season.

The name has a surprisingly gloomy origin. In the 1950s and 60s, police in Philadelphia called it 'Black Friday' because of the traffic jams and crowds of shoppers. Retailers later promoted a cheerful explanation: it was the day their accounts finally moved from loss ('in the red') to profit ('in the black').

What began as an American tradition has spread worldwide. Online shopping has stretched it into a long weekend that ends with Cyber Monday, and many shops in Taiwan now run their own Black Friday promotions alongside Singles' Day sales.

Not everyone is celebrating. Critics argue that huge discounts encourage impulse buying, debt and waste. In response, some people mark Buy Nothing Day, which started in Canada in the 1990s, by refusing to shop at all.
Economists also note that some 'deals' are not as good as they look, because prices are sometimes raised before being cut.

c.title: The Ritual of the Bargain
text: Black Friday, which falls this year on November 27, has become a secular ritual of modern capitalism, complete with pilgrimages to shopping malls, nocturnal queues and the devotional refresh of online carts.

Its name reveals how marketing can rewrite history. The phrase was originally a complaint from Philadelphia police in the mid-twentieth century, who dreaded the gridlock the day produced. Retailers later rebranded it with a tidier story about ledgers turning from red to black, an explanation that sounds plausible but appeared long after the original usage.

The event's expansion is a case study in cultural export. Carried by multinational brands and e-commerce platforms, it now competes in Asia with home-grown festivals such as Singles' Day, and it has lengthened into a 'Cyber Week' of near-continuous promotion.

Behavioural economists are sceptical of its benefits. Urgency, scarcity and countdown clocks exploit predictable biases, nudging shoppers towards purchases they would not otherwise make, while some advertised discounts are calculated from inflated reference prices.
Movements such as Buy Nothing Day offer a counter-ritual, though their influence is modest. Perhaps the most useful response is simpler: treating the bargain not as an obligation but as a decision.

b.title: Beauty, Water and Too Many Visitors
text: Venice is one of the most extraordinary cities on Earth. Spread across more than a hundred small islands in a lagoon off Italy's northeast coast, it is connected by canals and hundreds of bridges, and there are no cars at all.

The city was founded by people seeking safety in the marshes, and it grew into a rich trading republic. Its builders drove millions of wooden piles into the mud to support stone palaces, churches and the famous St Mark's Square.

Today Venice faces two serious threats. The first is water: exceptionally high tides, called acqua alta, regularly flood the streets. In 2020 a system of movable barriers known as MOSE began rising from the seabed to protect the lagoon during dangerous tides.
The second is overtourism. Millions of visitors arrive each year, while the number of people living in the historic centre has fallen below 50,000.
In 2024 the city began charging day-trippers an entry fee on busy days, an experiment that divides opinion among residents and visitors.

c.title: A City That Should Not Exist
text: By any sensible engineering standard, Venice should not exist. A city of marble and brick rests on soft lagoon mud, supported by forests of wooden piles that, starved of oxygen beneath the waterline, have hardened rather than rotted over the centuries.

It was improbability that made the city great. Refugees from the mainland settled the marshy islands for protection, and their descendants built a maritime republic that dominated Mediterranean trade for centuries, leaving behind the palaces and churches that now fill guidebooks.

Two pressures now threaten that inheritance. Rising seas and a slowly sinking city make the acqua alta floods more frequent; the MOSE barriers, operational since 2020, can seal the lagoon during extreme tides, but at great cost and with ecological side effects.

Tourism poses a subtler danger. As short-term rentals replace homes, the resident population of the historic centre has dwindled below 50,000, while visitors number in the millions. Critics warn of a 'Disneyfication' in which Venice survives as a stage set rather than a city.
The entry fee for day-trippers introduced in 2024 is an admission of the dilemma: how do you protect a place that everyone loves to death?

topic: Pangu Creates the World

a.title: The Giant Who Made the World
text: This is an old Chinese story about how the world began.
Long, long ago, everything was mixed together inside a huge egg. Inside the egg, a giant named Pangu was sleeping.
One day, Pangu woke up and broke the egg. The light parts floated up and became the sky. The heavy parts sank down and became the earth.
Pangu stood between them and pushed the sky up. Every day he grew taller, and the sky went higher. This went on for 18,000 years.
When Pangu died, his body became the world. His breath became the wind, his eyes became the sun and moon, and his blood became the rivers.
Many cultures have stories like this to explain where the world came from.

b.title: From Chaos to Mountains and Rivers
text: Before there was heaven or earth, according to Chinese myth, the universe was a dark, shapeless chaos contained in something like a cosmic egg. Inside it, the giant Pangu slept and grew for 18,000 years.

When Pangu finally awoke, he split the egg apart. The light, clear elements rose to form the sky, while the heavy, cloudy elements settled to form the earth, an image often linked to the ideas of yin and yang.

Afraid that the two might join again, Pangu stood between them, holding the sky up with his hands and pressing the earth down with his feet. Each day he grew taller, pushing them further apart, until they were fixed in place.

Exhausted, Pangu lay down and died, and his body was transformed into the natural world. His breath became the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder, his eyes the sun and moon, his blood the rivers, and his hair the stars and plants.

Written versions of the story appear in texts from the third century, but it was probably told aloud long before. Its message is striking: the world we live in was made from a single act of self-sacrifice.

c.title: A Body Becomes a World
text: Creation myths reveal what a culture considers fundamental. In the Chinese story of Pangu, recorded in texts from around the third century but almost certainly older, the cosmos begins not with a command but with gestation: undifferentiated chaos, enclosed like an egg, slowly nurtures a giant.

When Pangu awakens and cleaves the egg, the cosmos sorts itself by weight and clarity. The light and pure ascend as heaven; the heavy and turbid descend as earth, a division that later thinkers readily associated with the complementary forces of yin and yang.
Pangu's role is less that of an all-powerful creator than of a labourer. For eighteen millennia he braces the sky apart from the earth, growing with the task until the separation holds.

His death completes the work. In a striking act of transformation, his breath becomes wind, his eyes sun and moon, his limbs mountains and his blood the rivers, so that the familiar landscape is, in effect, his body redistributed.
The myth thus suggests an intimate kinship between humanity and nature: the world is not a machine assembled from outside, but the remains of a being who gave everything to make it.

a.title: A Day to Say Thank You

b.title: More Than Turkey
text: On the fourth Thursday of November, which this year falls on November 26, tens of millions of Americans travel home for Thanksgiving. It is one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

The holiday is usually traced to 1621, when English colonists in Plymouth, often called the Pilgrims, shared a three-day harvest feast with around ninety men of the Wampanoag nation led by Massasoit. The two groups had formed an alliance, and the Wampanoag had helped the newcomers survive their first year.

Thanksgiving became a national holiday much later. In 1863, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a day of thanks to help unite the country, and in 1941 Congress fixed it on the fourth Thursday of November.
Today traditions include turkey dinners, parades, American football and the President 'pardoning' a turkey at the White House.
For many Native Americans, however, the day is a reminder of the land, lives and cultures they later lost. Since 1970, some have gathered on Thanksgiving for a National Day of Mourning.
In this way, the holiday holds both gratitude and painful memory.

c.title: Gratitude and Its Shadows
text: Few holidays are as cherished or as contested as Thanksgiving, which Americans celebrate this year on November 26. For most families it is an uncomplicated ritual of travel, food and gratitude; for many Native Americans it is an annual reminder of dispossession.

The popular origin story centres on 1621, when the Plymouth colonists and members of the Wampanoag nation shared a harvest feast. The meal was real, but its later depiction as a harmonious beginning obscures the context: an alliance forged partly out of mutual need, after epidemics had devastated Wampanoag communities, and followed within decades by war and land seizures.

The holiday's national form owes more to the nineteenth century than to the seventeenth. Lincoln's 1863 proclamation sought unity in the middle of civil war, and the image of the 'first Thanksgiving' was popularised afterwards as a story about national identity.
Since 1970, some Native activists have marked the day as a National Day of Mourning, insisting that memory include those for whom colonisation was catastrophe.
These perspectives need not cancel each other out. Gratitude may be most honest when it acknowledges the costs on which a shared present was built.
